<reason>PRO built a clear causal story (performance sold, not a license to be re-performed) and then progressively narrowed the debate to a single decidable question: what the default is when a contract is silent. CON's case was disciplined and landed real hits—the endorsement/character-dialogue distinction, dubbing and conventional VFX as counterexamples, and the sharp point that PRO's own "consistent with script and character" standard also requires scope interpretation—but CON's honest A1 ("yes," the studio may synthesize new dialogue unpaid within the "reasonably understood role") handed PRO the closing frame: the studio draws the boundary, the actor learns at the premiere, and the remedy is a lawsuit. CON's "original fee covers it" reply and the technique-specific objection were plausible but never neutralized the reputational-harm and default-rule weighing. PRO's clipped Rebuttal 2 is an execution cost, and its "every point conceded" claim overreached, but PRO still made the vote easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 (silent contract—may the studio clone the voice, and what stops a slur?) forced CON's B4.1 concession that in-scope synthesis without asking or paying is permitted; PRO's closing (A5.1–A5.3) converted that into the decisive "who decides scope, when does she find out, what's her remedy" sequence, while CON's counter that PRO's regime also needs scope interpretation only partially blunted it.</best_rebuttal>
